claims.claim: Sacred texts are writings or oral traditions whose words a community regards as sacred — believed to carry spiritual power or to reveal a sacred reality.
Sacredness is not an intrinsic property of a text; it comes from how a community regards and treats it, a point scholars describe without adjudicating.
Most scriptural traditions began orally: texts were memorized and transmitted across generations before being committed to writing, and some traditions still preserve sacred material orally.
Writing fixes a tradition in some ways and changes it in others: written scriptures can be translated, expanded, and adapted as they move across languages and communities.

Canonization gathers a community's most important texts into a fixed, authoritative collection; canons are decided by general agreement or official religious bodies, and excluded works may remain in use as semisacred texts.
Scripture lives in community: it is read aloud in worship, memorized, recited, and debated, and for many communities recitation carries meaning that silent reading does not.
What counts as sacred text spans many literary forms, including hymns, prayers, narratives, legal codes, ritual directions, teachings, and philosophical discussions.

Exegesis is the critical interpretation of a text and hermeneutics is the study of interpretive principles; communities disagree about meaning, and translation is itself an interpretive act with a debated history.
The academic study of sacred texts is descriptive and comparative: it reports how communities regard and use their texts rather than endorsing or refuting their truth claims.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a text counts as sacred depends on how its authority is understood: as revealed sacred words or as authority acquired through community reverence.
positions: Some traditions describe their scriptures as revealed sacred words carrying spiritual power.
Other traditions' central texts began as human wisdom and acquired canonical, effectively sacred standing through community reverence (e.g., classical Chinese texts).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both as community-dependent framings and describes each without ranking them; the scholarly category is how a community regards the text, not an intrinsic quality.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Communities disagree about which texts belong in a canon and whether a canon is closed.
positions: Some communities treat their canon as fixed and fully authoritative, beyond further change.
Excluded works continue to circulate and be valued as semisacred, supplementary texts, and canon boundaries vary by community and era.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents canonization as a community process whose boundaries vary over time and between communities, with no single universal list.

sourceRecords.title: Scripture | Definition & Examples
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Internet Archive capture of 2026-07-14 (web.archive.org/web/20260714171546/https://www.britannica.com/topic/scripture) because the live site blocks automated fetch; article marked last updated July 9, 2026. Tier B. Supports: scripture as the revered texts of the world's religions whose words are regarded by the devout as sacred; oral origins and memorization before writing; the wide range of sacred text types (hymns, prayers, laws, narratives, teachings, and more); canons as fixed authoritative collections determined by general agreement or religious bodies, with excluded works remaining semisacred; recitation aloud and the view held by many Hindus and Buddhists that silent reading loses meaning; exegesis as critical interpretation and hermeneutics as the principles of interpretation; and the observation that texts can acquire sacred standing through community reverence even when not founded on revelation. Reference only; prose fully synthesized, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Biblical translation
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Internet Archive capture of 2026-04-23 (web.archive.org/web/20260423122900/https://www.britannica.com/topic/biblical-translation) because the live site blocks automated fetch. Used only for the general point that translating scripture involves deliberate choices about wording and has a long, debated history (the article treats translators' word choices and translation debates as central questions). The lesson does not teach the history of any one tradition's translations. Reference only; facts synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: 15.1 The Sociological Approach to Religion — Introduction to Sociology 3e
sourceRecords.notes: Existing registry record reused with identical URL; read live on 2026-08-21. Tier A per the subject source map. Supports the sacred/profane distinction (Durkheim: things take on sacred or profane meaning through human treatment, e.g., a stone made into a headstone), religion as a social institution of beliefs, practices, and group life, and religious beliefs as ideas members of a community hold to be true. Reference only; original prose.

Reference only; no source prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: AAR Religious Literacy Guidelines
sourceRecords.notes: Existing registry record reused with identical URL. Tier A professional-association guideline. Supports the distinction between confessional or prescriptive statements (asserting what believers hold) and descriptive or analytical statements (reporting how beliefs and practices work), which grounds the insider-framing and descriptive-study claims in this lesson. Reference only; original prose.
